subject: Geography
sub_topic: Important lakes — Chilika, Loktak, Wular, Dal, Sambhar

concepts.name: Chilika Lake: Formation, Type, and Hydrological Character
key_dimensions: Classification as a brackish-water lagoon (not a freshwater lake) — a common UPSC trap
Formation by longshore drift creating a sand bar separating it from Bay of Bengal
Seasonal variation: freshwater influx from rivers (Daya, Bhargavi) vs. saline intrusion from sea
Distinction between lagoon vs. lake vs. backwater — comparative geography angle

concepts.name: Chilika Lake: Ramsar Status and Ecological Significance
key_dimensions: First Indian wetland to be designated a Ramsar site (1981) — 'first' trap
Removal from Montreux Record (2002) after ecological restoration — significance of this action
Role as a critical habitat for migratory birds (Irrawaddy dolphins, flamingos) on Central Asian Flyway
Chilika Development Authority (CDA) — institutional mechanism and its mandate

concepts.name: Loktak Lake: Floating Phumdis and Unique Ecology
key_dimensions: Largest freshwater lake in Northeast India — directional qualifier trap (not 'India')
Phumdis: heterogeneous mass of vegetation, soil, and organic matter — unique to Loktak
Keibul Lamjao National Park: world's only floating national park, located on a phumdi
Habitat of Sangai (brow-antlered deer) — critically endangered species connection

concepts.name: Loktak Lake: Conservation Conflicts and Ramsar Listing
key_dimensions: Listed as Ramsar site (1990) and placed on Montreux Record due to ecological degradation
Ithai Barrage on Manipur River — impact on phumdi ecology and fishermen livelihoods
Conflict between hydropower interests (NHPC) and ecological conservation
Loktak Protection Act, 2006 — controversy over eviction of lakeside communities

concepts.name: Wular Lake: Tectonic Origin and Geographic Context
key_dimensions: Largest freshwater lake in India (and one of largest in Asia) — 'largest freshwater' trap vs. Loktak (NE India only)
Tectonic origin — formed due to tectonic activity in Kashmir Valley (not glacial)
Fed by Jhelum River; acts as a natural flood moderator for Kashmir Valley
Location in Bandipora district, Jammu & Kashmir — geopolitical sensitivity

concepts.name: Wular Lake: Tulbul Navigation Project Controversy
key_dimensions: India's plan to build a barrage (Tulbul/Wular Barrage) for navigation on Jhelum
Pakistan's objection under Indus Waters Treaty, 1960 — storage vs. navigation distinction
Project stalled since 1987 — ongoing bilateral dispute angle
Indus Waters Treaty provisions on 'western rivers' and Pakistan's rights — legal overlap

concepts.name: Dal Lake: Urban Wetland and Ecological Pressures
key_dimensions: Classification as an urban lake / Himalayan lake in Kashmir Valley
Dal is not a Ramsar site — negative fact trap (unlike Chilika, Loktak, Wular)
Eutrophication due to sewage, horticulture runoff, and floating gardens (Rad)
Dal Lake Authority and Supreme Court interventions for encroachment removal

concepts.name: Dal Lake: Floating Gardens and Traditional Land-Use
key_dimensions: Rad (floating gardens) — traditional agricultural practice unique to Dal Lake
Demb: areas of marshy land reclaimed for horticulture — land-use change pressure
Houseboats as cultural heritage vs. pollution source — dual-use conflict
Comparison with phumdis of Loktak — both are floating biomass structures but ecologically different

concepts.name: Sambhar Lake: Saline Nature, Origin, and Economic Significance
key_dimensions: Largest inland saline lake in India — qualifier 'inland saline' is critical
Origin: tectonic depression in the Aravalli foothills, Rajasthan
Salt production: major source of salt in India (Hindustan Salts Limited operates here)
Seasonal character: ephemeral lake — fills during monsoon, dries partially in summer

concepts.name: Sambhar Lake: Ramsar Designation and Flamingo Ecology
key_dimensions: Designated Ramsar site (1990) — one of few saline Ramsar wetlands in India
Critical habitat for flamingos (lesser and greater) — migratory bird significance
2019 mass flamingo mortality event — algal bloom / avian botulism — environmental disaster angle
Conflict between salt extraction industry and wetland conservation obligations

concepts.name: Comparative Classification: Freshwater vs. Saline vs. Brackish Lakes
key_dimensions: Freshwater: Wular (largest in India), Loktak (largest in NE India), Dal — hierarchy trap
Saline: Sambhar (largest inland saline); Pangong Tso, Tsomoriri — other saline lakes comparison
Brackish/Lagoon: Chilika — neither fully fresh nor fully saline
UPSC trap: confusing 'largest freshwater lake' (Wular) with 'largest lake in NE India' (Loktak)

concepts.name: Lakes and Ramsar Convention: India's Wetland Obligations
key_dimensions: Montreux Record: Loktak listed (still on record); Chilika removed (2002) — status difference
Ramsar sites among the five lakes: Chilika (1981), Loktak (1990), Sambhar (1990), Wular (1990) — Dal is NOT listed
Criteria for Ramsar listing vs. criteria for Montreux Record — conceptual distinction
National Wetland Conservation Programme (NWCP) linkage with Ramsar obligations

concepts.name: Drainage Basin and River Connectivity of Major Lakes
key_dimensions: Chilika: fed by Daya and Bhargavi rivers (Mahanadi delta tributaries), drains to Bay of Bengal
Wular: fed and drained by Jhelum River — part of Indus basin
Loktak: connected to Manipur River basin; Ithai Barrage altered natural flow
Sambhar: endorheic/closed basin — no outflow to sea; rivers Mendha, Rupangarh feed it

concepts.name: Pangong Tso and Tsomoriri: High-Altitude Trans-boundary Lakes
key_dimensions: Pangong Tso: extends across India (Ladakh) and China (Tibet) — about 60% in China
Tsomoriri: entirely in India (Ladakh), Ramsar site — distinction from Pangong
Both are saline, high-altitude tectonic lakes — different from Himalayan glacial lakes
Strategic significance: Line of Actual Control (LAC) passes through Pangong Tso — geopolitics-geography overlap

concepts.name: Lakes Formed by Different Geological Processes: Comparative Origin
key_dimensions: Tectonic origin: Wular, Sambhar, Pangong Tso — formed by crustal movement/subsidence
Lagoon/coastal origin: Chilika, Pulicat — longshore drift and bar formation
Fluvial/ox-bow origin: Kanwar (Bihar), Kabar Taal — meander cutoff lakes
Glacial origin: Tsongmo (Sikkim), Gurudongmar — meltwater lakes in high altitudes

concepts.name: Pulicat Lake: Comparison with Chilika as Coastal Lagoon
key_dimensions: Second largest coastal lagoon in India after Chilika — size ranking trap
Spans Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu — inter-state boundary conflict over jurisdiction
Sriharikota Island separates Pulicat from Bay of Bengal — geographic feature
ISRO's Satish Dhawan Space Centre on Sriharikota — geography-current affairs overlap

concepts.name: Lakes and Biodiversity Hotspots: Threatened Species Connection
key_dimensions: Sangai deer (brow-antlered deer) — Loktak/Keibul Lamjao exclusive habitat; Schedule I of Wildlife Protection Act
Irrawaddy dolphin — Chilika Lake population; IUCN status (Endangered)
Flamingos at Sambhar and Chilika — migratory congregation points on Central Asian Flyway
Wular Lake: Marbled teal, Baer's Pochard (critically endangered ducks) — lesser-known angle

concepts.name: Human Encroachment and Shrinkage of Lakes: Policy and Legal Response
key_dimensions: Dal Lake: National Green Tribunal (NGT) and Supreme Court orders on encroachment and houseboat regulation
Chilika: Aquaculture encroachment by prawn farming — CDA's role in eviction and restoration
Loktak: Illegal settlements on phumdis — Loktak Protection Act 2006 vs. community rights conflict
Wular: Encroachment for agriculture and willow plantation reducing lake area by ~50% since 1900

concepts.name: Lakes in Context of National Water Policy and Wetland Rules 2017
key_dimensions: Wetland (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 — replaced 2010 rules; state-level Wetland Authority mandate
No-go zones around Ramsar sites — 50m to 500m buffer zone provisions
Distinction: lakes regulated under Wetland Rules vs. rivers under Water Acts — jurisdictional clarity
Role of National Wetland Conservation Programme (NWCP) in lake restoration funding

concepts.name: Seasonal and Ephemeral Nature of Indian Lakes: Hydrological Variability
key_dimensions: Sambhar: ephemeral — seasonal filling and drying cycle affects salt crystallization
Chilika: seasonal salinity gradient shift — higher salinity in dry season, lower in monsoon
Loktak: water levels affected by Ithai Barrage regulation — 'controlled' seasonal fluctuation
Climate change impact: shrinkage of high-altitude glacial lakes vs. flooding of lowland lakes — contrast
